content: The response rates following treatment were consistently high, achieving ≥95% across all age groups and for the primary pangenotypic direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens. Older Children (6–11 years): Among 472 older children included in 13 study arms: 73 received sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks. 56 received glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8, 12, or 16 weeks. 34 received sofosbuvir/daclatasvir for 12 weeks. 178 received sofosbuvir/ledipasvir for 12 weeks. Nearly all participants were non-cirrhotic, with only three exceptions. The majority were treatment-naïve, with only seven having prior treatment experience. Most were infected with non-genotype 3 HCV. Sustained virologic response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12) was 99% overall (95% CI: 97–100%), with minimal heterogeneity: 100% (94–100%) for sofosbuvir/daclatasvir. 93% (86–98%) for sofosbuvir/velpatasvir. 96% (90–100%) for glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. 100% (97–100%) for sofosbuvir/ledipasvir. Adverse events were reported in 53% of children (226 out of 472), but none were classified as serious. Treatment discontinuation occurred in 1% (4 out of 490 children), with three cases attributed to adverse events (auditory hallucinations, drug-related rash, and headache). The strength of evidence was moderate for sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, and sofosbuvir/ledipasvir, but very low for other DAA regimens due to inconsistency and imprecision. Younger Children (3–5 years): Among 167 younger children included in seven study arms: 41 received sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks. 25 received glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 or 12 weeks. 56 received other regimens. All but one child were non-cirrhotic and treatment-naïve. SVR12 was achieved in 95% overall (95% CI: 89–99%), with no evidence of heterogeneity: 83% (70–93%) for sofosbuvir/velpatasvir. 92% (77–100%) for glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (96% in the DORA study Part 2). 99% (93–100%) for sofosbuvir/ledipasvir. No data were available for sofosbuvir/daclatasvir in this age group. The lower SVR12 rate for sofosbuvir/velpatasvir was due to seven treatment discontinuations caused by difficulties in taking the oral medication, not virological failure. Adverse events were reported in 72% of children (92 out of 128), with the most common being vomiting (21%), cough (14%), and diarrhea (9%). Treatment discontinuation was higher in the sofosbuvir/velpatasvir arms due to poor palatability of the oral formulation. The strength of evidence was moderate for sofosbuvir/ledipasvir and very low for other DAAs (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir). Pharmacokinetics and Dosing: Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir (400 mg/60 mg) is the preferred pangenotypic DAA regimen for adults and adolescents in many lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) due to its high efficacy and availability as low-cost generics. However, there is no direct study data on its efficacy and safety in children aged 3–5 years. Extrapolation of efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetic (PK) data from studies in adults, adolescents, and older children is a well-established regulatory practice. This approach is supported when the disease course and treatment response are expected to be similar across age groups. PK modeling and simulation studies suggest that the adult dose of sofosbuvir/daclatasvir (400 mg/60 mg) can be used in children weighing at least 25 kg, and a half-dose (200 mg/30 mg) can be used for those weighing 14–25 kg, potentially down to 10 kg. PK data from 17 HCV-infected adolescents in Egypt receiving sofosbuvir/daclatasvir were used to develop models predicting safe and effective dosing in children weighing 10–<35 kg. Monte Carlo simulations confirmed that daclatasvir 30 mg once daily achieves appropriate exposure in children weighing 14–<35 kg and even down to 10 kg. Two complementary studies assessed sofosbuvir PK in children relative to adults to establish appropriate dosing. Sofosbuvir exposures in children aged 6–<12 years were within predefined PK equivalence boundaries (50–200%) compared to adults, although Cmax was higher. Treatment Recommendations: The Guidelines Development Group strongly recommends treating all adolescents and children aged 6–11 years with chronic hepatitis C infection, regardless of disease stage, based on high/moderate certainty of evidence. A conditional recommendation is made for treating children aged 3–5 years, based on moderate/very low certainty of evidence. Early treatment in childhood and adolescence offers the potential to cure HCV before disease progression, preventing liver damage and extrahepatic manifestations. It also reduces transmission, stigma, and neurocognitive dysfunction, improving school performance and quality of life. Treatment with DAAs in children and adolescents (3–17 years) is highly effective and safe, with SVR12 rates ≥95% across all age groups for key pangenotypic regimens (sofosbuvir/daclatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, sofosbuvir/velpatasvir). Serious adverse events and treatment discontinuations were uncommon. However, younger children experienced more issues with treatment discontinuation due to poor palatability and adverse effects, making the benefit-to-harm ratio slightly lower in this group. Quality of Life: HCV infection in children negatively impacts quality of life, increasing caregiver stress, family strain, and impairing psychosocial and cognitive functioning. Studies show that achieving SVR12 with DAA treatment improves health-related quality of life scores in children and adolescents. Future Directions: Two efficacy, safety, and PK studies of sofosbuvir/daclatasvir in children <12 years are planned in Egypt and Cambodia to validate optimal dosing for regulatory approval and country adoption.
